summary: Presents procedures for creating and documenting Internet standards on routing protocols, established by the IAB with the IESG. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 4794.

eli5.summary: These are the steps a routing rulebook had to go through to become official. It is now out of date.

subtitle: The checklist a new routing protocol had to pass to become a Proposed, Draft or full Internet Standard.

tldr.problem: Routing protocols are complex, widely distributed, real-time algorithms that are hard to implement and test, so a protocol that works in one setting can fail in another or when it reaches an unforeseen limit.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets out, for each of the three standardization stages, the specifications, MIB, security architecture, implementations, testing, operational experience and reports that a routing protocol must supply.
tldr.outcome: The requirements grow stricter at each stage. This informational memo is now Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 4794.

today: RFC 1264 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 4794. It is an informational memo and no longer describes the current process.

sections.title: Why Routing Protocols Get Extra Scrutiny
sections.content:
RFC 1264 gives more specific guidance for advancing routing protocols through the three-stage Internet standardization process run by the IAB with the IESG. The stages are Proposed (a well written, openly reviewed specification), Draft (Proposed status, multiple implementations and some operational experience) and full Internet Standard (Draft status and more extensive operational experience). All levels are covered.

The memo recognises two kinds of routing protocol: Interior Gateway Protocols (IGP, also called intra-domain routing protocols) and Exterior Gateway Protocols (EGP, also called inter-domain routing protocols). It uses the terms IGP and EGP.
sections.eli5: Getting a routing rulebook approved works like earning belts in a sport. This memo says what you must show for each belt.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
The motivation is two-fold. The first aim is to reduce the risk of serious technical problems after a routing protocol reaches Draft Standard. The second is to ensure that the new protocol supports the continued growth of the Internet, which the memo describes as growing at an exponential rate.

The memo explains that a protocol may work in one environment with one implementation without working in a different environment with multiple vendors. It may also work well within a range of topologies and numbers of routers, then fail when an unforeseen limit is reached. Even with considerable operational experience, maturity is hard to guarantee.
sections.eli5: A bridge that holds a few bicycles might still collapse under a truck. The checks try to find that out before everyone drives across.

sections.title: General Requirements and Reports
sections.content:
The general requirements are seven items: specification documents good enough that independent, interoperable implementations can be built without consulting the original developers; a MIB so the protocol can be managed remotely; a security architecture that includes mechanisms for authenticating routing messages; several interoperable implementations, at least two written independently; evidence that all features have been tested between at least two implementations; operational experience; and two reports.

The first report documents how the requirements were met, including implementation experience, the MIB reference, the authentication mechanisms, a list of implementations, test results and a description of operational experience. The second report summarizes the key features and analyzes how the protocol will perform and scale, compared with existing protocols such as RIP and EGP where appropriate. It should say how much link bandwidth, router memory and router CPU the protocol uses, how that scales (including topologies at least an order of magnitude larger than the current environment), where the protocol will break, and which environments suit it.

The IESG sends its recommendation on advancement to the IAB based on the specifications and the reports.
sections.eli5: The team has to show a clear rulebook, a way to check on the routers, a lock against cheaters, and proof it works on more than one kind of machine. It also has to write down when it would stop working.

sections.title: Proposed Standard and Draft Standard
sections.content:
For Proposed Standard, the specification must be implementable by others, and the MIB must be at least an Internet Draft (it need not be submitted at the same time). The security architecture must be set out explicitly. One or more implementations must exist, and there must be evidence that the major features have been tested. No operational experience is required at this stage. A single report covers the key features, suitable environments, authentication, the MIB, implementation experience, implementations and test results.

For Draft Standard, the documents must be revised to reflect experience, with a section summarizing the changes, and the MIB must be at the Proposed Standard level. Two or more interoperable implementations must exist, at least two written independently, and all features (including the security features) must have been tested between at least two implementations. There must be significant operational experience in the operational Internet, in a moderate number of routers in a moderately complex topology, exercising all significant features. An IGP must carry both interior and exterior routes unless another mechanism is provided for exterior routes, and an EGP must carry the full complement of exterior routes. Both reports are required.
sections.eli5: The first belt only needs a working example and a good plan. The second belt needs several builders, real use on the live network, and a report on how big it can grow.

sections.title: Full Standard and Security Considerations
sections.content:
For full Standard, the documents are revised again, but only to clarify the protocol or guide implementers; no significant changes may be made at this stage. The MIB must be submitted for Standard at the same time as the protocol. Three or more interoperable implementations must exist, at least two written independently, and all features must be tested between at least two independently written implementations.

Operational experience must be significant: a large number of routers in a complex topology, part of the operational Internet, including multi-vendor operation. The second report is a revision of the Draft Standard report describing the additional knowledge gained since then.

The memo's Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo. Security enters through the requirement for an authentication-capable security architecture in the protocols being judged.
sections.eli5: The top belt needs even more builders, a big busy network, and no big last-minute changes to the rules.
